analysis.one_liner: Gives consumers stronger rights to see, correct, and limit use of their credit files, and reins in credit repair scams.
analysis.headline: The House passed the bill by voice vote on June 13, 1994, but the Senate never brought it up, and it died when the 103rd Congress ended on January 3, 1995.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would rewrite the Fair Credit Reporting Act to force credit reporting agencies to let consumers see their entire file, dispute and delete inaccurate information, learn who has pulled their report, and opt out of prescreened credit solicitations. It would require lenders to stop reporting information they know is wrong, ban reporting of debts from periods when a consumer was on disaster assistance or unemployment benefits, and impose contract and no-advance-payment rules on credit repair companies. It also adds FBI access to consumer reports for counterintelligence cases and preempts some stronger state consumer credit laws.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary consumers benefit most: anyone denied credit, insurance, or a job because of a wrong credit report would gain the right to see the whole file, learn who pulled it, dispute errors with a 30-day reinvestigation deadline, and get free reports in certain cases (after adverse action, if unemployed, on public assistance, or a fraud victim) [S3][S4]. Consumers could opt out of lists sold for prescreened credit offers through a toll-free system [S4]. People receiving disaster assistance or unemployment compensation could have missed payments during that period excluded from their file [S3][S4]. Job applicants would have to give written consent before an employer pulls a report, and medical information could not be shared without consent [S3][S4]. Victims of credit repair scams would get written contracts, a 3-day cancellation right, and class-action and FTC enforcement [S3][S4].

how_it_helps.text: Credit bureaus must disclose everything in a consumer's file, identify who procured reports and why, and provide a summary of consumer rights with each disclosure [S3][S4].

Bureaus must reinvestigate disputed items free of charge within 30 days and delete information that is inaccurate, incomplete, or cannot be verified, with procedures preventing deleted items from silently reappearing [S4].

Furnishers of information — mostly banks and lenders — are barred from reporting information they know or should know is incomplete or inaccurate, must tell bureaus when a consumer voluntarily closes an account, and must investigate disputes [S4].

Consumers can opt out through a toll-free notification system from having their names sold for prescreened credit offers, and reports generally cannot be furnished for direct marketing the consumer did not initiate [S3][S4].

Payments missed while a consumer was receiving federal disaster assistance or unemployment compensation can be excluded from the file at the consumer's request if the account has been current for a year [S3][S4].

Credit repair organizations face a new federal regime: no fees before services are performed, written signed contracts, a 3-business-day cancellation right, voided waivers, civil liability with punitive damages and class actions, and FTC enforcement [S3][S4].

Employment credit checks require clear written disclosure and the consumer's written authorization, and are limited to jobs requiring security clearances, fidelity bonds, or handling substantial cash or fiduciary duties [S4].

analysis.who_pays: Consumer reporting agencies (the credit bureaus) bear the largest compliance burden: toll-free lines, full-file disclosure, 30-day reinvestigations, opt-out systems, and reseller verification rules [S4]. Banks, lenders, and other furnishers face new duties to report accurately, flag disputes, and investigate within fixed deadlines [S4]. Direct marketers lose access to consumer reports for solicitations the consumer did not initiate [S3]. Creditors and insurers lose the ability to pull employment-purpose reports broadly and to share reports containing medical information without consent [S3]. The bill also preempts some stricter state laws, which reduces the regulatory burden compared with a patchwork of state rules [S4].

drawbacks.text: The bill preempts state laws on prescreening, dispute deadlines, adverse-action duties, and obsolete-information rules, blocking states from adding stricter protections unless they explicitly opt back in after January 2003 — trading some existing state-level consumer safeguards for one federal floor [S4].

It does not ban prescreening; instead of stopping the sale of consumer lists for unsolicited credit offers, it legalizes 'firm offers of credit' and only gives consumers the right to opt out [S3][S4].
It creates a new channel for the FBI to obtain consumer reports for foreign counterintelligence investigations by court order, without the consumer's knowledge during the investigation [S3].

New duties on furnishers of information are written with an explicit liability limitation — the civil liability provisions of sections 616 and 617 do not apply to violations of the furnisher-accuracy duty except through FTC/state enforcement paths, weakening private enforcement against banks [S4].
An honest supporter would acknowledge the compliance burden falls on credit bureaus and thousands of data furnishers, with real costs in a 455-day implementation window [S4].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit — consumers finally able to see their full file, force deletion of unverifiable information, and stop banks from reporting data they know is wrong — addresses a real, widespread harm: inaccurate credit files determine who gets credit, insurance, housing, and jobs. The main costs are compliance costs for bureaus and lenders, which are modest relative to the consumer benefit. The genuine design weaknesses are the state-law preemption, the choice to regulate rather than restrict prescreened marketing, the liability carve-out for data furnishers, and the new FBI access provision — each of which trims back the consumer benefit in favor of industry or government interests.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed the bill by voice vote under suspension of the rules in June 1994, but the Senate never voted on it and it died when the Congress ended in January 1995.

narrative.text: Rep. Esteban Edward Torres introduced the bill in the House on February 18, 1993, and it was referred to the House Banking, Finance and Urban Affairs Committee [S1][S6].
The bill attracted 33 cosponsors — 27 Democrats and 6 Republicans [S5].
The Consumer Credit and Insurance Subcommittee forwarded an amended bill to the full committee by a 17-12 vote on November 19, 1993, after holding hearings [S6].
The full committee ordered the bill reported, amended, by a 29-20 vote on March 3, 1994, and it was reported on April 28, 1994 [S6].
On June 13, 1994, Chairman Henry Gonzalez moved to suspend the rules and pass the bill, and the House agreed by voice vote [S6].
The Senate received the bill on June 14, 1994, read it twice, and placed it on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders (Calendar No. 461) [S6][S4].
No further Senate action was taken; the bill never received a Senate vote, and the 103rd Congress ended on January 3, 1995 [S6][S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Credit bureaus, banks, and direct marketers were better off because the bill died: they avoided new duties to report accurate information, toll-free consumer access, opt-out systems, and restrictions on selling consumer lists. Consumers who would have gained rights to see and correct their files got nothing from this bill.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Credit bureaus, banks, and direct marketers

sides.party_line_note: Support was bipartisan but Democratic-leaning: 27 of 33 cosponsors were Democrats and 6 were Republicans, the House passed it by voice vote with no recorded party split, and the committee votes (17-12, 29-20) do not break down by party in the record.

industries.note: The bill imposes heavy new duties on them — full-file disclosure, 30-day reinvestigations, toll-free lines, opt-out systems — but it also legalizes their prescreening business by defining 'firm offers of credit' and letting consumers only opt out rather than banning the sale of consumer lists, locking in that revenue stream. The preemption of state rules also gives them one national standard instead of stricter state laws.

industries.industry: Banks, lenders, and other furnishers of credit information
industries.note: They face new duties to report accurate information, flag disputed data, and investigate consumer disputes on fixed deadlines, but with an explicit carve-out limiting their private civil liability. They also remain the main users of prescreened credit offers, which the bill permits.

Title II bars them from charging before performing services, requires written contracts, grants a 3-day cancellation right, voids waivers, and exposes them to punitive damages and class actions with FTC enforcement — directly targeting companies that profit from consumers with damaged credit.
The bill bars furnishing consumer reports for direct marketing transactions the consumer did not initiate, cutting off access to mailing lists built from credit files.

Employers must disclose and get written consent before pulling an employment report, and may only use reports for sensitive positions — but employment agencies get an exemption from the consumer-report definition for job-procurement communications with consent safeguards.
